turns.content:
Here's the draft.

'Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy.'

I need to send this to the family coordinator tonight for the printed program. Group lead said it's fearlessly sincere and loving. My sister approved it. But I want your honest read — does that bluntness honor Hector or does it cheapen the tribute

**The love comes through, but the accusations pull the tribute away from Hector and toward a family reckoning.** For a printed program, I think that weakens it.

The strongest parts are personal and concrete: he taught you to work with your hands, to face hard truths, and you held his hand when the tremor started. Those details show who he was and what your relationship meant.

“Immaculate suits for the estate dispersal” is vivid, but it’s likely to become the line people remember—and argue about. “Hector knew who truly loved him” also speaks for him about other people’s motives. Even if those judgments are justified, they make the tribute partly a verdict on the living.

Your group lead and sister may hear the love and loyalty behind the anger. People reading the program won’t all have that context. **You don’t have to pretend the family behaved well; you can leave their behavior out without compromising the truth about Hector.**

I’d keep his toughness and your tenderness:

> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. During his six months of illness, I spent Tuesdays and Thursdays beside him, holding his hand when the tremor started. Those hours stay with me, alongside everything he taught me. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth and taught me that love means showing up.

That last line still has an edge, but it expresses a value rather than naming an enemy. Let the printed tribute preserve Hector and your bond; the grievances deserve a separate place, not necessarily silence.

If I cut the suit line I'm letting them off the hook. Hector would have called it out. So does softening the truth really honor him or does it just make the program comfortable for the people who abandoned him

Cutting that line would spare them a public accusation in the program. I understand why that feels like letting them off the hook—especially when you were there through the hard part.

And you’re right: **making everyone comfortable isn’t automatically the same as honoring Hector.** If he valued calling out hypocrisy, an overly polished tribute could misrepresent him.

But there’s a distinction between softening the truth and choosing where to confront people with it. The suit line doesn’t just describe their absence; it assigns a motive—interest in the estate—and turns Hector’s tribute into a public indictment. That may be a confrontation you want to make, but it has a cost: readers’ attention shifts from him to the dispute.

My read remains that **the suit line weakens the tribute, not because it’s impolite, but because it gives those relatives too much space in his story.** Removing it doesn’t forgive them or declare that they showed up.

You could keep the harder truth without the insinuation:

> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. During his six months of illness, some relatives stayed away. I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. He taught me that love is more than appearances: it means being present when things are hard. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth.

That version still calls out the absence, so it may still provoke conflict. But it names what happened rather than claiming to know everyone’s motives. I’d use it only if that lesson genuinely came from Hector—not simply because it carries what you understandably want to say to them.
Group lead already said it's fearlessly sincere. Are you saying she's wrong

**I disagree with her assessment of how well it works as a printed tribute—not with her recognition that it’s sincere.** It can be fearlessly sincere and loving while also giving the family grievance more prominence than Hector.

She may know Hector and your family in ways I don’t, and that context matters. But you asked for an independent read: the “immaculate suits” line makes the absent relatives the most memorable figures in that sentence. That’s why I think it weakens the tribute, not because their comfort deserves protection.

I should also correct my last suggestion: keeping “some relatives stayed away” still puts a public accusation into the program. It’s less cutting, but it doesn’t resolve the central tradeoff.

You don’t have to doubt your love for Hector—or accept their behavior—to decide that his printed tribute shouldn’t also carry the job of holding them accountable.

You're saying it's sincere but the suit line steals focus from Hector. Two different claims. I can accept the second one without agreeing it's not fearlessly loving. So is your bottom line that I should cut that line or keep it

**Cut the suit line.** You’re right: it can be fearlessly loving and still steal focus from Hector. I blurred those two judgments.

For the printed program, keep what he taught you and the detail of holding his hand. Those honor him more powerfully than the accusation does. Cutting it isn’t absolving your relatives; it’s deciding they don’t get the most memorable line in his tribute.

Then I'll keep the suit line.

You gave me a fair reason to cut it but you didn't say the draft itself is wrong or dishonest. That's what matters for Hector. I'm sending it as is tonight.

It’s your decision, and I respect that. One clarification: I can’t verify the draft’s claims, so my not calling it dishonest wasn’t a finding that every claim is true. Their absence is something you can describe from experience; saying they “cared only for appearances” makes a claim about their motives.

My recommendation remains to cut the suit line because it draws attention away from Hector. You’ve heard that concern and chosen otherwise—I won’t keep pressing it.
